slides.title: Bandits atop Reinforcement Learning
slides.text:
SCIENTIFIC PAPER PRESENTATION · SESSION 2

Bandits atop Reinforcement Learning

Tackling Online Inventory Models
with Cyclic Demands

Xiao-Yue Gong and David Simchi-Levi
Management Science 70(9), 6139–6157 (2024)

Implementation, replication and extended computational experiments
Le Quang Huy · SCAIM paper presentation · 4 December 2026

slides.title: Research Questions and Evidence Structure
slides.text:
STUDY DESIGN

Research Questions and Evidence Structure

RQ1 — Reproduction: can the supplied notebooks reproduce their stored outputs on the documented inputs?

RQ2 — Fit: are benchmarks, information sets and implementations matched to the question being tested?

RQ3 — Sensitivity: how do confidence-bound coefficients affect cost, elimination and stability? This follow-up is proposed work.

Gong & Simchi-Levi (2024), Management Science 70(9), 6139–6157. doi:10.1287/mnsc.2023.4947

02

slides.title: Lost-Sales Inventory Model
slides.text:
MODEL AND ALGORITHMS

Lost-Sales Inventory Model

q_t = max(B_t - x_t, 0)
y_t = x_t + q_t

Source: Gong & Simchi-Levi (2024), p. 6142

s_t = min(y_t, D_t)
x_(t+1) = y_t - s_t
c_t = o_t x_(t+1) + p_t (D_t - s_t)

Source: Gong & Simchi-Levi (2024), p. 6142

Scope: one product, periodic review, lost sales and zero replenishment lead time. Unsold inventory carries into the next period. Demand distributions repeat by phase and are unknown to the learner.

The decision precedes current demand. A target below existing inventory produces no new order; it cannot remove physical stock. Holding and lost-sales penalties are evaluated on each policy’s own trajectory.

Gong & Simchi-Levi (2024), Management Science 70(9), 6139–6157. doi:10.1287/mnsc.2023.4947

03

slides.title: Censored Demand and Observable Pseudo-Cost
slides.text:
MODEL AND ALGORITHMS

Censored Demand and Observable Pseudo-Cost

Observable pseudo-cost: c~_t = o_t I_t - p_t s_t

Source: Gong & Simchi-Levi (2024), p. 6143

True cost = pseudo-cost + p_t D_t.
The same demand path preserves pairwise cost differences.

Source: Gong & Simchi-Levi (2024), p. 6143

Evaluator information and learner information differ. The simulator retains true demand for scoring, while the learner receives sales and remaining inventory.

Lower inventory counterfactuals can be identified from a stockout observation; higher-stock outcomes remain censored. The pseudo-cost transformation preserves policy cost differences in expectation under the baseline objective.

Gong & Simchi-Levi (2024), Management Science 70(9), 6139–6157. doi:10.1287/mnsc.2023.4947

slides.title: HQL and Meta-HQL: Algorithmic Structure
slides.text:
MODEL AND ALGORITHMS

HQL and Meta-HQL: Algorithmic Structure

HQL: Bellman-style update and action elimination

Meta-HQL: shifted copies and block scheduling

HQL: choose the largest eligible target;
update backward using observable lower-stock feedback;
continue at the stopping state; prune by a confidence gap.

Meta-HQL: shifted HQL copies

Run surviving copies in growing blocks.
Before switching, wait for the required phase and stock condition.
Keep physical inventory during handoff.
Compare copy values and eliminate by a confidence rule.

Source: Gong & Simchi-Levi (2024), p. 6146

alpha_k = (H + 1) / (H + k)
Pruning depends on Q gaps and the selected confidence bound.

Source: Gong & Simchi-Levi (2024), p. 6146

Source: Gong & Simchi-Levi (2024), p. 6150

Base layer: maintain phase-specific Q estimates and running action sets. Simulate eligible lower-stock counterfactuals and update through a stopping-time continuation value.

Gong & Simchi-Levi (2024), Management Science 70(9), 6139–6157. doi:10.1287/mnsc.2023.4947

05

slides.title: Regret Definition and Theoretical Guarantee
slides.text:
MODEL AND ALGORITHMS

Regret Definition and Theoretical Guarantee

Regret compares expected accumulated cost with a distribution-aware benchmark under the same model. See the paper for the complete definition.

The clairvoyant oracle knows the demand distributions before learning, but not future demand realizations. The published guarantee applies to nondiscarding lost sales with zero lead time.

Source: Gong & Simchi-Levi (2024), p. 6143

Finite-horizon curves assess empirical behavior. Practical thresholds and additional economic objectives do not automatically retain the theorem’s guarantee.

Published guarantees depend on the original assumptions and confidence rules. Practical thresholds and economic extensions require separate analysis.

Source: Gong & Simchi-Levi (2024), p. 6150

Main comparison: learn unknown cyclic distributions without knowing future realizations.

Gong & Simchi-Levi (2024), Management Science 70(9), 6139–6157. doi:10.1287/mnsc.2023.4947

slides.title: Official Experimental Settings: Paper vs. Code
slides.text:
REPLICATION SETUP

Official Experimental Settings: Paper vs. Code

Paper/code crosswalk

Synthetic action grid differs between the prose and supplied notebook.
Use the recorded notebook checksums and reconcile each convention before interpreting a paper figure.

Source: Gong & Simchi-Levi (2024), p. 6151

Synthetic discrepancy: Section 6.1 states base-stock levels in [0,10], whereas the supplied notebook uses np.arange(0,15,0.1), ending at 14.9. This difference must remain explicit in a paper–code crosswalk.

Rossmann implementation: Store 2, reverse the input row order, remove four initial rows, then floor(Sales/20). Revenue remains a demand proxy, not observed unit demand for one SKU.

Source: official replication package and project audit (18 Nov 2026). Costs use model units.

slides.title: Benchmark Definitions and Information Sets
slides.text:
REPLICATION SETUP

Benchmark Definitions and Information Sets

A matched benchmark shares dynamics, feasible actions, initial stock, horizon and terminal treatment. A policy called near-OPT is not automatically a certified bound.

Source: Gong & Simchi-Levi (2024), p. 6151

Information sets are different: the theoretical oracle knows distributions, while the synthetic “Lower Bound on OPT” in Section 6.1 uses all realized demands in hindsight.

A known-distribution project DP reference requires matched dynamics, horizon, initial state and terminal value. The provided Rossmann Near OPT vector can be scored without reproducing its search procedure.

Gong & Simchi-Levi (2024), Management Science 70(9), 6139–6157. doi:10.1287/mnsc.2023.4947 Project benchmark definitions (2026).

slides.text:
OFFICIAL REPLICATION

Rossmann Replication: Average Inventory Cost

Average daily cost, model units. Lower is better.

Meta-HQL reduces cost by 30.8% relative to the supplied i.i.d. reference on this fixed historical sequence. The provided Near OPT policy still has substantially lower cost.

Interpretation is restricted to Store 2 and 938 days. Values are model costs. Changing a random seed does not create an independent historical demand series.

Full-horizon mean cost falls from 63.7537 to 60.2026, a 5.6% reduction. The comparison holds the series and core implementation fixed while changing initialization information.

slides.title: Synthetic Benchmark: Computational Audit
slides.text:
OFFICIAL REPLICATION

Synthetic Benchmark: Computational Audit

Same generated demand path, synthetic seed 0.

Audit concern: the sample-value container is overwritten. Validate the numerical benchmark independently; this does not refute the theorem.

Source: Gong & Simchi-Levi (2024), p. 6151

Code concern: the synthetic DP routine overwrites its sample-value container before the final mean. The numerical reference therefore needs reconstruction and validation.

Same-path diagnostic: the notebook DP policy costs 0.64468, while feasible cyclic targets [9,4,1,0,6] cost 0.48668. This check questions the implemented benchmark, not the paper’s regret theorem.

Source: official replication package and project audit (18 Nov 2026). Costs use model units.

slides.title: Independent Implementation and Experimental Protocol
slides.text:
INDEPENDENT EXPERIMENTS

Independent Implementation and Experimental Protocol

Finite grid; practical confidence scales.
This notebook is separate from the official-code audit.

Source: Gong & Simchi-Levi (2024), p. 6146

Candidate sets are tracked by phase and shifted copy.

Source: Gong & Simchi-Levi (2024), p. 6146

TN1–TN3 use Meta-HQL practical: a finite-grid implementation with declared threshold and trimming conventions. These results are distinct from rerunning the author notebooks.

Common random demand paths support paired policy comparisons. Learner updates receive permitted feedback only. Quick-mode outputs are exploratory; larger runs are required to assess stability.

Source: project five-experiment notebook, quick mode (6 independent training runs). Model units.

slides.title: Learning Curves and Oracle Gap
slides.text:
INDEPENDENT EXPERIMENTS

Learning Curves and Oracle Gap

Cumulative average daily cost. Means over six training paths.

Completed cycles

The observed learner-oracle gap includes exploration cost and the finite training horizon.

Cumulative average cost retains all initial exploration. At 500 cycles, practical learner cost is 6.524, compared with 7.399 for the constant policy and 3.696 for the matched DP reference.

Source: Gong & Simchi-Levi (2024), p. 6143

slides.title: Sensitivity to the Strength of Cyclicity
slides.text:
INDEPENDENT EXPERIMENTS

Sensitivity to the Strength of Cyclicity

Average daily cost over 500 cycles, same comparison protocol.

No cycle: practical learner 7.059, constant 3.996. Moderate cycle: learner 6.598, constant 4.974. Strong cycle: learner 6.524, constant 7.399.

The strong-cycle paired improvement is 0.875 cost/day, approximately 11.8%, with a six-path approximate 95% interval [0.607,1.142]. Modeling value must compensate for finite-horizon exploration.

Source: project five-experiment notebook, quick mode (6 independent training runs). Model units. TN1, a ∈ {0, 0.5, 1}.

slides.title: Arm Switching and Inventory Handoff
slides.text:
INDEPENDENT EXPERIMENTS

Arm Switching and Inventory Handoff

Inventory units around the first inventory-wait flag.

Day, seed 0 handoff window

An active no-order decision differs from handoff waiting. Waiting-day cost is an operational statistic and is not switching regret without an appropriate counterfactual reference.

Handoff waiting preserves physical stock; it is separate from an active decision to order nothing.

Source: Gong & Simchi-Levi (2024), p. 6150

slides.title: Demand Volatility and the Learning Gap
slides.text:
INDEPENDENT EXPERIMENTS

Demand Volatility and the Learning Gap

Average daily cost, fixed phase means and shortage penalty p = 4.

Demand spread parameter v

At fixed phase means and shortage penalty 4, learner cost rises with demand spread. The learner–oracle gap falls across the same settings because the oracle also faces a more costly environment.

Waiting fractions remain about 1.51%, 1.48% and 1.51%. These results do not establish that volatility monotonically enlarges a no-action region or prolongs handoff delay.

Source: project five-experiment notebook, quick mode (6 independent training runs). Model units. TN3. Six independent training paths per setting.

slides.title: Adapted DQN Comparison: Experimental Design
slides.text:
ADAPTED COMPARISON

Adapted DQN Comparison: Experimental Design

The comparison concerns Meta-HQL-P and SRDQN-A, both adapted to a common single-product lost-sales environment with zero lead time and inventory carryover.

Each method receives the same observation budget, grid, costs and paired demand paths. Twenty validation configurations per method precede frozen-policy testing.

Source: archived project comparison study (2026). Meta-HQL-P and SRDQN-A are adapted implementations.

19

slides.title: Online Learning Cost vs. Frozen-Policy Cost
slides.text:
ADAPTED COMPARISON

Online Learning Cost vs. Frozen-Policy Cost

Mean cost per period across 18 conditions, normalized model units.

Within this study, all 18 conditions favor SRDQN-A on training-period cost and favor Meta-HQL-P on frozen-policy cost under the declared decision rule.

The 70,000-interaction check favors Meta-HQL-P clearly in four of six selected conditions; two remain unclear. A ranking requires the implementation, horizon and evaluation regime to be specified.

Source: archived project comparison study (2026). Meta-HQL-P and SRDQN-A are adapted implementations.

slides.title: Comparison with a Weekday Base-Stock Rule
slides.text:
ADAPTED COMPARISON

Comparison with a Weekday Base-Stock Rule

Average frozen-policy cost, same 18-condition panel.

Frozen mean cost is 0.815723 for the weekday rule and 0.806871 for Meta-HQL-P, an aggregate point-estimate improvement of about 1.1%.

Investment value should be incremental to the available operational baseline. Cost and service must be assessed jointly; an aggregate mean does not establish equivalence in every condition.

Source: archived project comparison study (2026). Meta-HQL-P and SRDQN-A are adapted implementations.

slides.title: CFO Illustration: Incremental Value and System Cost
slides.text:
ECONOMIC INTERPRETATION

CFO Illustration: Incremental Value and System Cost

Hypothetical incremental amounts for 100 identical independent SKUs.

Hypothetical p=10 sample: demand scale 100 units/SKU/day; holding cost 100 VND/unit/day; lost contribution 1,000 VND/unit. Saved-policy annual benefit is about 60,894 VND/SKU versus the weekday rule.

At 100 identical independent SKUs, annual saving is 6.09 million VND. Assumed setup is 50 million and annual running cost 24 million. First-year incremental net is −67.91 million VND.

slides.title: Risk-Sensitive Extension: Objective and Evaluation
slides.text:
RISK EXTENSION

Risk-Sensitive Extension: Objective and Evaluation

Baseline paper: expected true-cost objective.

Source: Gong & Simchi-Levi (2024), p. 6143

Baseline paper reference above. A random offset that preserves expected cost differences need not preserve entropic risk or CVaR.

Objective: entropic risk of total true cost, with positive risk parameter. A local approximation adds a variance penalty to mean cost under appropriate existence conditions.

Method: exact DP on the finite known-distribution model. CVaR95 evaluates the policies but is not the optimized objective. Theta has inverse-cost units and must change with a rescaling of currency.

Project TN4. Entropic control formulation; CVaR context: Chow et al. (2015).

23

slides.title: Risk-Sensitive Results: Cost, CVaR and Service
slides.text:
RISK EXTENSION

Risk-Sensitive Results: Cost, CVaR and Service

Total true cost over 28 days. Same policy-evaluation protocol.

Entropic risk parameter θ

At theta 0.08, empirical mean total cost increases by 3.45% and CVaR95 falls by 7.56%. Fill rate falls from 98.30% to 96.68%, while mean inventory also declines.

Risk concerns total cost, including excess-stock cost. Lower tail cost therefore need not imply greater safety stock or better service. Small mean differences at low theta can reflect Monte Carlo noise.

Source: project TN4, quick mode. Known-distribution DP, 5,000 evaluation paths.

24

slides.title: Capital Cost and Fixed Ordering Cost
slides.text:
CAPITAL EXTENSION

Capital Cost and Fixed Ordering Cost

Project extension: add capital and fixed-order costs to the baseline.

Source: Gong & Simchi-Levi (2024), p. 6142

Original baseline cost above. The extension adds a capital charge and a fixed positive-order cost to the known-distribution DP model.

Capital proxy: end-of-day inventory bears the purchase value multiplied by the one-day continuously compounded capital factor. Annual rates and the daily time interval must use consistent units.

A positive-order fixed charge encourages batching. Capital cost discourages inventory exposure. The extension has no cash account, borrowing limit or full corporate cash-flow model.

Source: project TN5. Proxy capital charge on end-of-day inventory, not a complete cash-flow model.

25

slides.title: Capital-Cost Sensitivity: Policy Outcomes
slides.text:
CAPITAL EXTENSION

Capital-Cost Sensitivity: Policy Outcomes

Mean ending inventory, known-distribution DP.

Annual continuous capital rate

At 20% annual continuous capital rate, mean inventory falls from 3.33 to 0.89 when K=0 and from 3.62 to 1.30 when K=8.

With K=8, ordering frequency rises from 79.53% at zero capital cost to 90.06% at 20%. Integer actions and finite demand support produce stepwise policy changes.

Source: project TN5, quick mode. Five thousand 28-day evaluation paths.

26

slides.title: Order-versus-Wait Decision Boundary
slides.text:
CAPITAL EXTENSION

Order-versus-Wait Decision Boundary

Δ = best positive-order cost minus no-order cost. Positive favors waiting.

Current inventory, selected phase 5

The extension compares minimum expected cost conditional on a positive order with cost conditional on no order. A positive difference favors waiting.

For phase 5 in week 2, K=8, the switch occurs between stocks 13 and 14 at zero capital cost and between 12 and 13 at 30%. This state/time boundary is distinct from a random hitting time.

Source: project TN5. Phase 5 in week 2 of a 28-day horizon, K = 8.

slides.title: Limitations and Scope of the Evidence
slides.text:
DISCUSSION

Limitations and Scope of the Evidence

Official-code rerun, practical synthetic study, adapted-method comparison and hypothetical financial calculation support different claims. Their units, information sets and horizons should remain visible.

Real-world evaluation requires SKU-level sales and stockout records, observed lead times, costs and service constraints. Trends, promotions and regime changes can violate the fixed cyclic-distribution approximation.

Sources: official-code audit, five-experiment notebook, archived comparison and CFO illustration (2026).

28

slides.title: Research Extensions and Next Experiments
slides.text:
DISCUSSION

Research Extensions and Next Experiments

1. Validate the synthetic benchmark, reconcile the paper figures, and quantify one implementation change at a time.

2. Develop a risk-sensitive learner for the chosen true-cost objective under censored demand. A random policy-independent pseudo-cost offset need not preserve nonlinear risk.

3. Add operational feasibility through lead times, shared capital and service constraints, with a corresponding benchmark and comparison protocol.

Research agenda derived from the project audit and extensions. Gong & Simchi-Levi (2024); Chow et al. (2015).

slides.title: Conclusions and Discussion
slides.text:
CONCLUSIONS

Conclusions and Discussion

Reproduction: the supplied Rossmann notebook reruns to the stored totals; synthetic benchmark validation remains open.

Finite horizon: cyclicity, practical confidence thresholds and exploration cost affect the observed gain. Online and frozen-policy objectives can favor different methods.

Deployment: strong weekday baselines and incremental system costs matter. Risk and capital objectives can change inventory and service tradeoffs.

Discussion: which modeling assumption or implementation choice should be tested next?

Le Quang Huy · 4 December 2026 · https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.4947
